articles.title: San Francisco startup sends humanoid robots to clean homes for $30 an hour, but humans still control the machines remotely
articles.summary: US News: San Francisco tech startup Tau Robotics has, in a feat, launched AI robots that provide home and office cleaning services, including vacuuming floors,.
articles.body: San Francisco tech startup Tau Robotics has, in a feat, launched AI robots that provide home and office cleaning services, including vacuuming floors, clearing clutter, and taking out the trash. "Yeah, yesterday we made it public that we are starting to offer a cleaning service with humanoids in SF," Alex Koch, CEO and co-founder of Tau Robotics, told ABC News. The move puts the long-hyped promise of household robots to an early, public test, and it's already drawing skepticism from some robotics expert.How Tau Robotics' humanoid cleaning service worksTau Robotics, a San Francisco startup, has begun offering home cleaning services using humanoid robots, according to the company's CEO and co-founder, Alex Koch, who confirmed the launch. The pricing and scope are narrow for now, the company is offering the service for $30 an hour to a select group of applicants in San Francisco. On its own website, the company describes the offering similarly, pricing it at $30 per hour for each humanoid unit and noting that two robots work a job at a time, with access currently invite-only through a waitlist.Crucially, the robots aren't operating on their own. Koch said today's AI cannot yet fully control a humanoid robot by itself, instead, a human operator runs the robot remotely from a central location, with AI assistance. Tau Robotics' own site echoes this, describing its robots as "operated by humans and AI." That distinction matters for anyone picturing a fully autonomous machine let loose in their living room; what's actually being deployed is closer to a teleoperated robot with AI support layered on top.What these humanoid cleaning robots can actually doAccording to Koch, the robots are already handling some basic chores reasonably well. He said vacuuming is "working pretty well already," and that basic tasks like wiping a kitchen counter are "pretty doable" too.The company's site lists a similar, narrow set of tasks, such as, wiping down counters and tabletops, vacuuming hardwood floors and rugs (including along baseboards), taking out the trash, and clearing clutter or spills off the floor. It also advertises broader categories, that are, house cleaning, deep cleaning and office cleaning. Tau Robotics has also released videos showing the humanoid robots performing cleaning tasks, including one sped-up clip of a robot exiting a minivan before a cleaning job.Who can book Tau Robotics' humanoid cleaning service in San FranciscoKoch framed the launch less as a replacement for existing cleaners and more as a way to widen the market. He said many of the company's initial customers are people who either didn't previously use house cleaners or only hired human cleaners infrequently, meaning the service, in his view, mainly expands the overall market rather than displacing it.Consistent with that framing, the company says it is currently inviting a limited number of households to sign up, rather than opening the service broadly, with interested customers asked to provide their email and neighbourhood to join a waitlist.Why a UC Berkeley robotics professor is sceptical of humanoid home cleaning robotsNot everyone is convinced the technology is ready for prime time. Ken Goldberg, a UC Berkeley engineering professor with 40 years in the field, expressed scepticism in an ABC News interview about humanoid robots' current home-cleaning capabilities. He said it's "too early" and that he'd be surprised if the robots could do anything close to a genuinely useful cleaning job, noting that even picking objects up off the floor remains a challenge for robots, and that sweeping or wiping counters and areas underneath things is still very difficult.Goldberg also questioned how representative the company's promotional footage really is. He raised doubts about the prerecorded demonstration videos, pointing out that viewers can't tell whether footage has been sped up, whether a human was working behind the scenes, or whether the environment was carefully staged to make a single successful run possible.The current limitations and future of humanoid robots in home cleaningThe gap between the marketing reel and the messier reality of home cleaning is, in many ways, the story of humanoid robotics right now. Despite the open questions about what the technology can currently do, the broader ambition remains a humanoid robot capable of cleaning an entire home at low cost, a goal that, if realised, could make home cleaning services more widely accessible.For now, though, the San Francisco rollout looks less like a robot househelp moving in and more like a human-piloted machine, with AI in a supporting role, learning to vacuum floors and wipe down counters one job at a time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘This is a war’: South Africa battles femicide as women’s bodies pile up
articles.summary: Bodies of nine women have been found in a Johannesburg neighbourhood in two months, as worries grow over women’s safety.
articles.body:
A ninth woman has been found dead in South Africa’s Ekurhuleni municipality in about two months, intensifying concerns over violence against women and prompting renewed scrutiny of the government’s response to the country’s femicide crisis.

The latest victim was found on Thursday morning in Dawn Park, a residential area of Boksburg, east of Johannesburg. The woman is believed to be in her thirties and was found half-naked and wrapped in a sheet. Police are investigating the deaths but have not established that all nine cases are connected.

“We are still investigating whether we are dealing with one perpetrator or a group of men that are behind the murders of these women,” South African Police Service spokesperson Athlenda Mathe told the Reuters news agency on September 15.

Mathe said investigators were also examining whether copycat crimes could be involved, but stressed that police had so far found no links between the cases.

“This is not an investigation that you can rush, because it is quite complex,” she said. “It may at this stage involve multiple perpetrators. But let’s leave it to the detectives.”

‘It feels like individuals are being hunted’

Princess Eurika Mogane, a commissioner at South Africa’s Commission for Gender Equality, told Al Jazeera the killings reflected a broader crisis facing women across the country.

“This is a war. It feels like individuals are being hunted,” Mogane said. “When someone is the hunter, [the] best thing that you can do is to ensure that the prey are protected.”

The National Shelter Movement of South Africa (NSMSA) says its 24-hour helpline and affiliated shelters are seeing women arrive with increasingly severe experiences of abuse, including death threats, stalking, strangulation, coercive control and repeated violations of protection orders.

“These are not isolated incidents,” the organisation told Al Jazeera in an emailed statement. “They are indicators of a broader crisis in which violence against women has become deeply normalised in many communities.”

Police advice urging women not to walk or run alone and to avoid isolated areas following the killings has prompted criticism.

“A lot of the women in South Africa right now are saying, ‘You are basically telling us to adjust our lives to perpetrators,’” Mogane said.

The NSMSA said women alter their routes, avoid travelling at specific times, share their locations with loved ones and restrict their movements to try to stay safe.

“Safety messaging should not imply that women can prevent violence simply by making different choices,” the organisation told Al Jazeera. “The responsibility for violence lies with perpetrators, while the responsibility for protection lies with society and the state.”

Among the women discovered dead was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a 38-year-old mother and runner who disappeared after leaving home in the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg, for her usual run about 5:30 pm on September 9.

Her eight-year-old daughter raised the alarm when her mother did not return. Moselakgomo was found dead three days later on September 12.

Nokukhanya Khanyile-Lenake, a specialist paediatrician and mental health advocate, told Al Jazeera that women, as it is, take multiple precautions to protect themselves “from the dangers of gender-based violence”.

What particularly struck her, Khanyile-Lenake said, was that Moselakgomo’s eight-year-old daughter “knew the danger signs and did the right thing”, realising her mother had not returned and notifying other family members.

“And that still wasn’t enough,” she said. “As women, we’ve done the maximum to the point where we’re even teaching our young children what to do, and it’s still not enough.

“What I saw was a woman who chose to take care of herself and make a decision she’s probably made a thousand times before, which is just to go for a run,” Khanyile-Lenake added.

The killings come less than a year after South Africa classified gender-based violence and femicide as a national disaster in November 2025. South Africa’s parliament says the country’s femicide rate is five times the global average.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has pledged that perpetrators will face justice, while authorities say police patrols and deployments have been increased in high-risk areas.

But Mogane questioned what had materially changed since the national disaster classification.

“The declaration is there. But what progress has there been?” she said, pointing to the need for more forensic facilities and shelters for survivors.

The NSMSA said shelters continue to face inadequate and inconsistent funding, rising demand and capacity constraints, while survivors report delays in police responses and difficulties obtaining or enforcing protection orders.

Leaving an abusive relationship can itself be one of the most dangerous periods for a woman, the organisation said, with survivors often simultaneously needing police protection, emergency accommodation, transport, healthcare, childcare and financial support.

“For many women, the fundamental question remains unchanged: ‘If I leave today, can I survive financially, find safe accommodation, and remain protected from my abuser?’” the NSMSA said.

Al Jazeera asked the South African government what measures it has taken since the national disaster classification and for its response to criticism of its handling of violence against women, but had not received a response by the time of publication.

articles.title: She started a children's book company from her Los Angeles garage with $30,000; it grew to $5 million in annual revenue
articles.summary: US News: Carinne Meyrignac turned a simple idea sparked by motherhood into a children’s publishing business generating millions in annual revenue. After discov.
articles.body: Carinne Meyrignac turned a simple idea sparked by motherhood into a children’s publishing business generating millions in annual revenue. After discovering musical books in France that kept her young daughter engaged, she returned to Los Angeles and struggled to find similar products. In 2016, she decided to create her own interactive musical books, launching Cali's Books from her family garage. In an interview with Entrepreneur, Meyrignac explained how she travelled to China to meet manufacturers and invested about $30,000 in her first order of 6,000 books. What began as a small venture gradually expanded through direct-to-consumer sales, reaching $5 million in revenue by 2024.How Carinne Meyrignac started her children’s book company with $30,000Meyrignac said she wanted her daughter to develop a love of reading, but found that a baby focused on a conventional book could be difficult. The musical books she encountered in France offered a different experience by combining reading with sounds and music. She described them as “magical” because of how they captured her daughter's attention.After moving back to Los Angeles, Meyrignac noticed that the products available to her were different from what she had seen in France. She recalled finding mainly bulky plastic books with buttons on the side. That gap led her to develop books designed to be interactive for both children and parents. According to Cali’s Books official website, the products are interactive books to encourage children's interest in books and music, with sound and music built into the reading experience.Meyrignac travelled to China to produce the first lot of Cali’s BooksThe first major step was turning the concept into a physical product. Meyrignac travelled to China to meet manufacturers and placed an initial order of 6,000 books, investing approximately $30,000. She kept the operation deliberately small in its early stages. Rather than building a large team immediately, Meyrignac worked with freelancers found through Fiverr and relied on friends and family for help. The approach was “scrappy”, reflecting how she used outside help and personal networks while testing and developing the business.The company initially invested considerable effort in selling through physical shops. Meyrignac later said that the strategy created challenges, including lower margins and difficult payment terms. More importantly, she felt it reduced her ability to communicate directly with the parents and grandparents buying the books. The shift towards direct-to-consumer sales became an important stage in Cali’s Books' development. Selling online allowed the company to communicate directly with families, collect feedback and better understand how customers were using the books. Meyrignac told Entrepreneur that “everything unlocked” after moving towards direct-to-consumer, while the company has since returned to retail, including selling through Nordstrom.Cali’s Books reaches $1 million in revenue in 2020Cali’s Books did not immediately generate predictable revenue. Meyrignac said it took roughly three years for the company to achieve consistent monthly revenue. The turning point came as the business concentrated more heavily on direct-to-consumer sales. In 2020, Cali’s Books crossed the $1 million revenue mark.The company continued expanding after that milestone. Meyrignac told Entrepreneur that Cali’s Books reached $5 million in revenue in 2024 and continued growing at a double-digit pace. Reportedly, the company had sold around 700,000 books in the US alone, while its broader company profile describes more than 50 titles selling over 500,000 copies worldwide.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2022, Delaware sank the 180-foot Texas Star, once a floating casino and scallop vessel, at Redbird Reef as the state’s third reef ship in three years
articles.summary: US News: In June 2022, Delaware sunk the Texas Star, a former floating casino and scallop vessel, to enhance the Redbird Reef, boosting marine habitats and recreational opportunities.
articles.body: A 180-foot ship that once served as a floating casino and commercial scallop vessel found a final role off the Delaware coast in June 2022. The vessel, named the Texas Star, was deliberately sunk by Delaware's Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control (DNREC) to become part of an artificial reef system. Instead of being dismantled on land, the retired ship was prepared for life on the seafloor, where its steel structure could provide a new surface for marine life and create another destination for recreational fishing and diving.According to DNREC, the Texas Star was sunk on June 29, 2022, at Redbird Reef, about 16.5 miles offshore, where the water was approximately 86 feet deep. Its deployment was the third vessel sinking carried out by the state's reef programme in three years. The project was part of Delaware's wider effort to create underwater habitat in an area where the natural seabed is largely sand and mud.From supply ship to floating casinoThe history of the Texas Star can be traced back well before it sank to the bottom of the ocean. The ship was constructed in 1977 using the hull of a multi-purpose supply ship. During its career as a working ship, the ship was equipped as a floating casino and was used to catch scallops commercially. Before being sunk by Delaware, the Texas Star had been used in many different ways. Sinking the ship required more than simply towing it offshore and dumping it into the water. According to the DNREC, the vessel was sunk only after being cleared for environmental and safety standards by the US Environmental Protection Agency and US Coast Guard.The state invested $325,000 in federal Sport Fish Restoration funds to acquire the Texas Star from marine contractor Coleen Marine. The contractor carried out the sinking, which took place at around 4:20 p.m. local time. Once it settled on the seabed, the vessel became a permanent piece of the artificial reef rather than a working ship. The conversion illustrates one of the unusual ways retired infrastructure can acquire a second function. A ship that had once been designed to carry out industrial and commercial work was deliberately placed where its hull could provide three-dimensional structure in an otherwise relatively flat marine environment.A new structure on the seafloorRedbird Reef was already an unusual seabed before the Texas Star arrived there. This reef covers around 1.3 square miles. It is known for its collection of more than 700 retired New York City subway cars, which gave the reef its name because of their reddish paint. The reef also includes tanks, armoured vehicles, tugboats, fishing trawlers and barges.The purpose is not simply to create an underwater collection of unusual objects. Delaware's artificial reef programme uses stable, cleaned and non-toxic materials to create hard surfaces where marine organisms can attach and grow. Over time, those surfaces can become covered with organisms and provide shelter and feeding areas for fish. According to research published in PeerJ, scientists examining 12 artificial reef sites off the coasts of Delaware, Maryland and Virginia found that fish abundance was significantly associated with the amount of sea-whip coral growing on the reefs. The study also found that sea whips contributed much of the reefs’ vertical structure, adding complexity to the underwater habitat and providing additional surfaces and spaces for marine life.The third vessel in three yearsThe Texas Star marked an addition to a second wave of artificial reef development for Delaware. The state began establishing its reef sites as far back as 1995, and today there are 14 reef sites that have been permitted in Delaware Bay and the Atlantic Coast. The chain of vessels that were sunk included the Reedville first in August 2020 on Redbird Reef; this ship previously served as a Navy and Army freighter, and later as a menhaden fishing ship. This was followed by the sinking of the menhaden ship named John S. Dempster Jr. in early 2021 on the Del-Jersey-Land Reef.For Delaware, the reefs offer more than habitat for fish species. They also provide recreation for anglers and divers, giving retired vessels a new purpose. This artificial reef project, as described by its initiators, forms part of a wider plan to promote fisheries, recreational angling and diving, and tourism. Beneath the Atlantic waters, the ship became another addition to Delaware’s man-made reef structures, which are designed to provide habitat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Judge Judy warns of 'danger' if prosecutors don't retry Lindsay Clancy after murder trial ends in mistrial
articles.summary: Judge Judy Sheindlin says there's a "danger" in not retrying Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children.
articles.body: Judge Judy Sheindlin weighed in Thursday on the closely watched Lindsay Clancy murder case following its mistrial, warning there could be a "danger" in prosecutors deciding not to retry the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children. The 83-year-old judge and television personality was asked by TMZ whether Clancy should face another trial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict earlier this month. "I think there's a danger in that, in not retrying," Sheindlin responded. Sheindlin, who launched the popular syndicated show "Judge Judy," which aired for 25 seasons, was also asked about her view on the outcome of the trial after the jury's deliberations ended in a reported 11-1 split in favor of finding Clancy not criminally responsible. PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL "I can't give you a two minute answer on that," Sheindlin said. She was then asked whether she believed Clancy should have been found guilty. "There's no question, my dear, that she killed her children," Sheindlin said. "The only question is, is there an excuse for it? Make up your own mind on that one." DR PHIL SAYS LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL A 'TEACHABLE MOMENT' ON POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS: 'THERE WAS A FAILURE HERE' TMZ also asked Sheindlin about Rep. Nancy Mace's public call for Clancy to be publicly executed. "I think it's ridiculous," Sheindlin responded. Clancy's defense does not dispute that the 36-year-old former delivery room nurse strangled her three children with exercise bands in January 2023. Her defense has argued that she was not criminally responsible because of mental illness or defect. LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR DENIES BIAS ALLEGATIONS, WANTS 'CONVERSATION STARTED' ABOUT WOMEN'S MENTAL HEALTH Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after seven days of deliberations when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict. Several jurors later said 11 members of the panel favored finding Clancy not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, while one favored conviction. Immediately after the mistrial was declared, Clancy's longtime defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, signaled that he would fight another attempt to put her on trial. The defense has indicated it plans to argue that the circumstances surrounding the mistrial should bar a second trial. However, in a recent interview with Fox News' Bryan Llenas, Reddington said that if prosecutors reduced the top charge to second-degree murder, he would opt for a bench trial — one without a jury — in the hope that she would receive probation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Clancy remains in custody at Tewksbury Hospital and is due back in court Sept. 29. articles.title: In 2017, Charlie Puth paid $4.17 million for a Montecito home where he later married Brooke Sansone; nine years later, the 5,920-sq-ft property sold off-market for $18.5 million
articles.summary: News News: Singer-songwriter Charlie Puth, 34, has cashed out on his Montecito home where he married the love of his life, Brooke Sansone. The 5,920-square-foot .
articles.body: Singer-songwriter Charlie Puth, 34, has cashed out on his Montecito home where he married the love of his life, Brooke Sansone. The 5,920-square-foot property was sold off-market for $18.5 million, The Real Deal reported. In nine years since the purchase, Charlie Puth has more than quadrupled his money on the Montecito estate. The deal closed in July but was only recently made public. The off-market nature of the sale means neither price negotiation nor competing bids are part of the public record, which is common in the high-end California real estate market.Charlie Puth bought the property for $4.17 millionCharlie Puth purchased the Montecito property in 2017 for $4.17 million, when he was 25. The property holds quite the emotional weight for Puth. Just two years before the sale closed, he got married to Sansone. The couple exchanged vows on 7 September 2024, two years after they began dating. They grew up together in New Jersey. Their fathers attended elementary school together and reconnected years later. The couple earlier spoke about why they chose the Montecito mansion for the wedding. “We chose the Puth family residence because we just knew Montecito would offer the perfect backdrop,” the couple told Vogue.Sansone felt the home was the perfect setting for their union. “I wanted our wedding to marry tradition with modern unconventionality. I wanted each detail to feel relaxed yet perfectly, thoughtfully curated. Serving mini hot dogs on silver platters, for example, was more than just a fun detail. It was a reflection of my love for styles that blend the refined with the playful,” she told the publication.Nearly a decade after the purchase, Puth has sold the sprawling estate for more than four times that amount. The mansion was sold for $18.5 million. The buyer is a limited liability company tied to John Jarve, a partner at venture capital firm Menlo Ventures and founder of Sierra Point Capital, according to The Real Deal. Carolwood Estates’ Cameron Chesley and Shaun Alan Lee represented the seller, while Compass’ Gregoire & Beuoy Real Estate Group represented the buyer.Inside the Montecito mansionThe Montecito mansion on 1421 Wyant Road was sold for $3,125 per square foot. Spanning 5,920 square feet, the gated estate offers a high degree of privacy. Surrounded by mature landscaping, the mansion has six bedrooms and seven bathrooms. The residence features hardwood flooring throughout, along with a spacious kitchen. The layout flows towards courtyards and gardens, a Montecito hallmark designed for both intimate gatherings and larger entertaining.There has been a boom in Montecito real estate in the past couple of years, driven by post-pandemic migration, celebrity acquisitions and a scarcity of available land. After the pandemic, there were several high-profile restaurant openings. The small town, which has fewer than 10,000 residents, has seen its real estate market outperform much of Southern California. The median home price in Montecito has climbed roughly 80% since 2019. Ellen DeGeneres flipped a villa in 2024 for a $32 million price tag. Oprah Winfrey sold off part of her sprawling compound to Adam Levine and Behati Prinsloo, who later listed their own Montecito estate for $65 million.For Puth, the portfolio moves are as much strategic. Over the past couple of years, he has juggled multiple California properties. Beyond the Montecito sale, he liquidated a Studio City property in May for $2.1 million, down from an initial asking price of $2.9 million. He had purchased that home in 2021 for $1.5 million. In October 2024, he sold his Trousdale Estates mansion in Beverly Hills to ‘Million Dollar Listing Los Angeles’ star Josh Flagg for $11 million. Puth had bought that residence in 2017 for $9 million.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.body: Protests broke out in a city in central Nigeria after 37 miners detained during raids on suspected illegal gold mines were found dead in the custody of the paramilitary force that carried out the operation.The Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) conducted the raids on September 15 and 16 in the Wushishi-Lukoto area, west of Minna, the capital of Niger State.The agency initially suggested that a suspected disease outbreak may have been involved in the miners' deaths. It later clarified that the cause of death had not been established and would be determined through medical examinations.Nigerian interior minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo ordered the immediate suspension of Niger State's NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending a full investigation."It is an unfortunate incident, however, a full investigation will be conducted while the commandant under whose watch this happened remains suspended," an interior ministry statement quoted him as saying.The mother of one of the detainees, Shafa'atu Suleiman, told reporters outside the hospital on Thursday that she had visited her son, Abdullahi, in detention and found him in a cramped NSCDC cell. She later learned that he had died.Officials had refused to allow relatives to deliver food to the detainees and demanded 100,000 naira ($75) for their release, the woman alleged."This is injustice. We will not forgive them."Anger over the deaths sparked protests in Minna on Thursday night, with youths chanting "Justice must be done", according to residents. Some protesters also damaged vehicles.By Friday morning, the city was calm, but security forces had been heavily deployed across parts of Minna.Nigeria has for years sought to curb unauthorised mining at thousands of informal sites across the country. articles.title: Surrey council staff refused anonymity for Sara Sharif inquest
articles.summary: A coroner rejects an application for three workers after the media, including the BBC, opposed it.
articles.body:
A coroner has rejected a request for anonymity made on behalf of three council workers who are expected to give evidence at the inquest into the death of Sara Sharif.

The 10-year-old was found dead in a bunk bed at her family home in Woking, Surrey, in August 2023.

Her father and stepmother – Urfan Sharif and Beinash Batool – were jailed for life in December 2024 after being found guilty of her murder.

At a pre-inquest review hearing last week, Surrey County Council applied to prevent the identities of the workers being reported by the press during the full hearing, but that application was resisted by media organisations, including the BBC.

Concerns were raised about Sara's care within a week of her birth in 2013, and her parents were known to social services as early as 2010, it has been reported.

Surrey County Council workers tried to visit the family home the day before she was murdered but visited the wrong address , a review also found.

It also found that services in Surrey failed to identify that Sara was at risk of abuse and did not question unexplained bruising.

This included a failure to properly investigate why she started wearing a hijab - that covered the bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Alethea Redfern, representing the council, said anonymity would protect the employees from "harm to their health and private and family lives".

She added there would be a "risk that the employees could no longer work if their identities were revealed", which would be a "loss of valuable resource" to the authority.

Senior coroner Richard Travers said: "I am not satisfied, on the basis of the evidence provided, that granting anonymity is justified by reference to common law principles of fairness."

He said that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights on respecting private and family life is balanced against Article 10 on the freedom of expression for the media, which Travers added was an "important principle of open justice".

The BBC, Times Media Limited, and Guardian News & Media Limited opposed the anonymity application.

Urfan Sharif was jailed for a minimum term of 40 years, while Batool has to serve at least 33 years in custody.

Sara's uncle, Faisal Malik, 31, was found guilty of causing or allowing her death and jailed for 16 years.

Sara died after a campaign of abuse, and a post-mortem examination found she had suffered dozens of injuries.

Surrey County Council has previously said it was "deeply sorry" after the review into Sara's case.

The full inquest is expected in October 2027.

articles.title: Bangalore Terriers complete 3-year J&K counter-terror tenure, return home
articles.summary: Defence News: BENGALURU: The 106 Infantry Battalion (Territorial Army) PARA, popularly known as the “Bangalore Terriers”, returned to Bengaluru on Friday after comp.
articles.body: BENGALURU: The 106 Infantry Battalion (Territorial Army) PARA, popularly known as the “Bangalore Terriers”, returned to Bengaluru on Friday after completing a three-year field tenure in Jammu & Kashmir, where it was deployed in a counter-terrorist operational environment.“The battalion was deployed in J&K from June 2023 to Sept 2026. During the tenure, it maintained a focus on battle drills, firing and Quick Reaction Team (QRT) exercises as part of its operational preparedness. The Army said the deployment was incident-free,” the ministry of defence (MoD) said on Friday.The battalion also won the Inter-Battalion Platoon Competition conducted under the aegis of the Formation Headquarters. Its training standards were appreciated by formation commanders in its chain of command.The battalion is currently commanded by Colonel Tejas B Candade, Sena Medal, of 2 PARA (Special Forces), who took over in August 2025.Welcoming the troops on behalf of the Karnataka govt, Bengaluru Development Authority chairman NA Harris thanked them for their service to the nation. BDA commissioner Major P Manivanan, who is also a Territorial Army officer serving part-time with the battalion, and Bengaluru Central City Corporation additional commissioner (Development) Venkatachalapathy R, were also present.The Bangalore Terriers, MoD said, returned with operational experience gained during the field tenure, enhanced training standards and renewed confidence.“Raised on Oct 1, 1960, at Jalandhar Cantonment, the battalion was initially affiliated with the Punjab Regiment. It moved its permanent location to Bengaluru in 1966 and was affiliated with the Parachute Regiment on April 1, 1979,” MoD added.The battalion has also served in earlier military and humanitarian operations. During the 1965 Indo-Pak war, its troops captured 36 Pakistani SSG commandos near Adampur in Punjab. In 1999, it provided humanitarian assistance during the Odisha Super Cyclone as part of Operation Sahayta.

articles.title: Supermarket sold expired Chocos; consumer commission orders Rs 10,182 payout to customer
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Ludhiana district consumer commission has directed Vishal Mega Mart to refund Rs 182 to a customer after finding that an expired food p.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Ludhiana district consumer commission has directed Vishal Mega Mart to refund Rs 182 to a customer after finding that an expired food product was sold to him. The commission also ordered the retailer to pay Rs 10,000 as compensation and litigation costs and restrained it from selling or displaying expired products. The order was passed on September 8, 2026.Why did the customer complain against Vishal Mega Mart?According to the commission order, Rajwinder Singh visited the retailer’s Ludhiana store on December 1, 2025, and bought Kelloggs Multigrain Chocos Fills for Rs 182 along with other items. He paid Rs 228 through UPI. After reaching home, he noticed that the product carried a date of November 1, 2025. He alleged that the retailer had sold him an expired product and that it was unsafe for human consumption.The customer alleged that he informed the store but received no response. He then sent a legal notice on January 10, 2026, which also went unanswered. He approached the consumer commission seeking a refund of Rs 182, Rs 2 lakh as compensation and Rs 3,500 towards litigation expenses.The retailer denied any deficiency in service or unfair trade practice. It argued that merely producing a bill did not establish that the expired product shown by the customer was the same product purchased under that bill. It said the product could have been purchased earlier or from another store.The retailer also claimed that the complaint was part of a series of similarly structured cases and alleged that the customer and his associates were deliberately linking expired products with genuine bills to seek compensation. The retailer asked the commission to dismiss the complaint.What did the consumer commission find?The bench comprising President Sanjeev Batra along with member Monika Bhagat noted that the retailer had admitted issuing the invoice but had taken a tentative position about the identity of the product. It said the retailer could have produced details such as the batch number, manufacturing date and expiry date of the product sold under the invoice but did not do so.The commission also referred to the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It noted that the law treats the sale of food after its expiry date as a matter for which the seller can be held liable.“Further Section 2(9) (i) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 reads as under:- ‘(9) "consumer rights" includes,-- (i) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property’,” the commission noted.It held that the customer’s right to safety had been affected and said sellers and manufacturers have a legal obligation to ensure that products are safe and fit for their intended purpose.The commission further rejected the retailer’s argument that the product shown in the photographs might have come from another transaction. It observed that the retailer claimed to have inventory management and compliance systems but had not produced evidence that could have clarified the issue.“The assertion of the OPs though looks fanciful, but it is devoid of any merits or logic. Since the OPs have claimed that the maintenance of robust and well-established inventory management and compliance systems including automated billing and systematic stock retention mechanisms, the OPs could have very detect such alleged previous transaction by a click of the mouse, but no such evidence was brought before this Commission,” it further added.The commission held that the retailer was guilty of deficient service and unfair trade practice for selling the expired product. It directed Vishal Mega Mart to refund Rs 182 within 30 days of receiving the order. If the refund is not made within that period, the retailer will have to pay Rs 200 per day from the date of the order until payment, subject to a maximum of Rs 10,000.The commission also ordered the retailer to pay Rs 10,000 as composite compensation and costs. It directed the opposite parties to discontinue the unfair trade practice and restrained them from selling, displaying or exhibiting expired products for sale.“Therefore, the acts and omissions of the OPs have not only resulted in causing of monetary loss to the complainant, but the complainant has also suffered mental agony and shock. As such, the OPs are guilty of rendering deficient service and also adopted the unfair trade practice while selling the expiry product to the complainant,” the bench concluded.

articles.title: Ukraine fires drone barrage as Russia launches elections
articles.summary: Russia’s first parliamentary election since the invasion opens with no antiwar party on the ballot.
articles.body:
Ukraine has launched a barrage of drones on Moscow and other regions as Russia opened polls for its first parliamentary elections since the start of the war.

More than 350 Ukrainian drones targeted the Russian capital on Friday morning, Moscow’s mayor reported. With the vote potentially offering the Kremlin a measure of the public mood over the invasion, Kyiv has maintained its bid to use air attacks to have Russians feel the impact of the conflict politically, socially and economically.

Polls opened on Friday in the Far East, where Kamchatka and Chukotka on the Pacific became the first of Russia’s 11 time zones to vote in the three-day ballot for the 450 seats of the State Duma, the lower house of parliament.

Only political parties that back the war have been registered to run. Yabloko, the sole party opposing the conflict, was barred from the ballot in August.

Voting runs until 18:00 GMT on Sunday. Moscow has also organised balloting in occupied parts of Ukraine.

President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party, which has dominated Russian politics since 2000, is certain to win the most seats. However, the margin of its victory, and seats won by other parties, is being closely watched.

With protests banned and no antiwar candidates standing, the vote offers the Kremlin a measure of the depth of public support and frustration with a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands of people since February 2022.

Ukraine has found significant success in bringing the impact of the conflict home to Russians, with almost nightly drone attacks hitting energy and economic infrastructure, causing billions of rubles in damage.

Kyiv maintains, like Moscow, that it does not target civilians, but many civilian deaths have also been reported deep inside the country.

On Friday, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on social media that most of the 350 drones sent towards the capital overnight had been destroyed at an outer defensive perimeter, with 64 shot down as they approached the city.

As well as the barrage targeting Moscow, Ukrainian forces ⁠hit the Yaroslavl oil refinery overnight, ⁠President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported, adding that a strike ‌on a military airfield in Rostov had damaged military aircraft and helicopters.

“There have ⁠also been good results ⁠in the ⁠Black Sea,” ⁠he said on social media without giving details.

Russian forces also continue to use air strikes to destroy Ukraine’s economic and military infrastructure and disrupt support for Kyiv’s continued defence.

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Friday that its forces had struck a logistics hub belonging to Ukrainian postal company Nova Poshta near the Black Sea port city of Odesa, as well as a cargo vessel in the nearby port of Chornomorsk. It said both strikes had been for military purposes.

A Russian drone attack on Friday morning injured five people, including three children, in the Kyiv region, Governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.

Russia said the previous day that it had targeted three drone manufacturing facilities and the De Novo data centre – the “largest centre ensuring the operation of server equipment used for military purposes” – near Kyiv.⁠

articles.title: Israel is killing the people who could end its wars
articles.summary: From Iran to Gaza and Lebanon, assassinations have repeatedly removed figures capable of negotiating an end to conflict.
articles.body:
In international politics, it is often assumed that wars end when the fighting becomes unbearable and the parties turn to diplomacy. But diplomacy requires interlocutors — figures with the standing to negotiate and the authority to deliver. Remove them, and a war loses not only its potential mediators but the very possibility of a settlement.

This is worth keeping in mind after a striking recent assessment. In early September 2026, Sir John Sawers, the former head of Britain’s foreign intelligence service, told The Financial Times that Israel had deliberately killed Ali Larijani. In his reading, Larijani was targeted not because he ran Iran’s war effort, but because he was among the few Iranian figures capable of reaching a deal both sides could accept.

Coming from a career intelligence officer rather than an advocate, the judgement invites a larger question: does the killing of Larijani belong to a pattern in which Israel removes, at moments of possible negotiation, the very people through whom a war might have been ended?

Consider what such killings actually produce. Assassinating the head of a government or an army opens a vacuum that others rush to fill. Assassinating a designated negotiator opens a narrower and more damaging one: a vacuum of moderation.

The successor to a killed negotiator is rarely more flexible than the person removed. More often, he is harder, because the hardliners are the ones who survive and inherit. The channel loses its author, and the hardening that follows is then read, on both sides, as proof that diplomacy was never possible in the first place. The tactic becomes self-fulfilling: it does not merely interrupt a negotiation; it manufactures the evidence that negotiation was futile.

The precedent is old. In September 1948, Count Folke Bernadotte, the United Nations mediator for Palestine, was assassinated in Jerusalem by members of Lehi, the Zionist underground whose leaders included the future Israeli prime minister, Yitzhak Shamir. Bernadotte had been shuttling between the parties with truce and partition proposals. His killers regarded any compromise as betrayal.

The same logic reappeared in November 2020, when Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, the leading figure in Iran’s nuclear programme, was killed near Tehran in an operation widely attributed to Israel. The timing — weeks after Joe Biden was elected president of the United States, having committed to reviving the 2015 nuclear agreement — led many to read it less as counterproliferation than as an obstacle deliberately placed in the path of diplomacy.

Larijani’s killing in March 2026 fits the same template. He had been Iran’s nuclear negotiator two decades earlier and had defended the 2015 deal as speaker of parliament. After the assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on the war’s opening day, he had become the country’s effective decision-maker. Western diplomats who dealt with him described him as tough but pragmatic — precisely the kind of counterpart with whom an American off-ramp might have been negotiated.

This is not a method confined to states. Israel applies the same logic to the non-state actors it fights, and the results reveal both the strategy and its ambiguities.

In February 1992, Israel killed Hezbollah’s secretary-general, Abbas al-Musawi. His successor was Hassan Nasrallah, who, over three decades, built the movement into the most capable non-state armed force in the region — a vacuum filled by a far harder man. In July 2024, Israel assassinated Ismail Haniyeh, the head of Hamas’s political bureau and its lead negotiator in the Gaza ceasefire talks, while that diplomacy was still under way; authority passed to Yahya Sinwar, and the negotiating track never recovered. Weeks later, Israel killed Nasrallah himself.

In each case, the target was the point of coordination — the figure through whom the adversary organised and, at times, negotiated. Removing him produced the same short-term disarray and, at least twice, a successor even less inclined to a deal.

Seen through Israel’s own strategic lens, this is coherent rather than merely vindictive. For a state that regards Iran’s system as an existential threat, the preferred outcome is that system’s collapse, not a negotiated accommodation with it. A durable deal brokered by a credible pragmatist would stabilise the very order Israel wants to see fall, and it would foreclose the American military pressure on which the hope of collapse depends.

The effect is visible inside Iran itself. External pressure has tended to harden the very indecision it claims to break, widening the split between a political leadership that acknowledges the war’s costs and a security establishment that treats every strike as vindication of defiance. Removing the pragmatists tilts that balance further towards the second camp — and towards the conclusion that there is nothing left to negotiate.

Israel’s stated rationale, in each case, has been military and preventive: the decapitation of a hostile leadership. That claim is not baseless. Larijani was no dove — he helped run a war effort and presided over harsh repression at home. Haniyeh led a movement responsible for the October 2023 attack. The intent to foreclose diplomacy is inferred, not proven, and the returns are uncertain: as the al-Musawi killing showed, removing a leader can produce a stronger and more implacable successor rather than a pliable one.

Yet something more consistent runs beneath these cases. Eliminating politicians whose trajectories threaten Israel is not new; their complete removal has become almost a priority, on a par with waging the full-scale military war in which Israel believes it holds a decisive advantage over any adversary in the region and perhaps beyond.

But military superiority alone has not been enough. In the Iranian case, despite the devastation Israel and the United States have inflicted, Tehran has not raised the white flag. And this is where a second definition of victory takes shape: the manufacture of internal political chaos capable of driving the Iranian system towards complete political collapse. That, more than any single assassination, is the essence of Israel’s strategy in its war on Iran.

How that strategy ends is still uncertain. But if the figures capable of closing a deal are removed as fast as they emerge, and the centres through which adversaries govern and negotiate are hollowed out by design, one question becomes unavoidable: who is left to make peace with — and does a strategy that keeps winning on the battlefield by emptying the negotiating table eventually run out of anyone able to end the war at all?

articles.title: Surinder Koli: Man acquitted in India's Nithari murder case found dead
articles.summary: The 50-year-old was freed of all charges by the Indian top court in November last year.
articles.body:
A man who spent nearly two decades in prison over one of India's most notorious murder cases has died, months after he was released, according to media reports.

Surinder Koli, 50, was found hanged inside a tea stall he ran in Haridwar in the northern state of Uttarakhand, on Friday, reports say.

He was released in 2025 after India's top court acquitted him in the final case against him linked to the 2006 killings of women and children in Nithari, a village on the outskirts of Delhi.

His body has been recovered and an investigation launched, according to reports. The BBC has contacted police for comment.

The 2006 case shocked India after the remains of 19 women and children were found near a bungalow.

NDTV, quoting police said Koli was found hanged inside a tea stall on Friday morning, with no suicide note found at the scene.

Who killed our children? Indian parents ask as 'house of horrors' convict acquitted

Indian court frees men jailed for serial killings

When the case emerged, it sparked national outrage and questions over whether police had ignored complaints from families whose children had gone missing.

Koli and his employer, businessman Moninder Singh Pandher, were arrested in 2006 after body parts were found near Pandher's home in Nithari. Police alleged the murders took place there, where Koli worked as a servant.

The revelations triggered national outrage. Many parents accused authorities of ignoring complaints about the missing children for more than two years. The case also exposed India's deep social divides.

Many victims came from poor migrant families, while the bungalow where the men lived was in a more affluent part of the neighbourhood.

India's top investigative agency, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), filed 19 cases against the two men. Koli was accused of murder, kidnapping, rape and destroying evidence, while Pandher was charged with immoral trafficking.

In 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted Koli in 12 cases. Pandher was also acquitted in two cases that year and released.

In November last year, the Supreme Court acquitted Koli in the final case, ruling that his confession - which included claims of cannibalism and necrophilia - had been extracted under torture. He was set free after 19 years in prison.

After his release, Koli reportedly moved to Haridwar, where he had been running a rented tea stall for the past few months.

articles.title: Rapper Cam Meekins and his brothers pooled $1,000 to make English muffins in a Boston apartment; the food business now has over 3,000 retail locations
articles.summary: US News: Cam Meekins spent his early career as a recording artist signed with Atlantic Records, producing, writing and performing his own music while touring a.
articles.body: Cam Meekins spent his early career as a recording artist signed with Atlantic Records, producing, writing and performing his own music while touring across the US. He later turned those skills towards a very different venture: English muffins. Meekins told Entrepreneur that he and his brothers Kyle and Nick started Stone & Skillet in 2014, pooling $1,000 to buy a mixer and flour and making muffins in Kyle's Boston apartment. The company's own website, however, dates the creation of its original recipe to 2013, making the exact founding year unclear across sources. What began as a small side project has since become a family-owned packaged food company with national distribution across more than 3,000 retail locations. Its products are sold through chains including Whole Foods Market, Publix, Wegmans and Fresh Thyme. In a 2025 Entrepreneur interview, Meekins said the business had become an eight-figure company after reaching its first $100,000 month in its second year. A $5 million Series A announced in May 2026 is now funding further expansion.The English muffins began in a Boston apartmentAccording to Meekins' account to Entrepreneur, his brother Kyle had the idea of selling premium English muffins to Boston restaurants known for elaborate Sunday brunch menus. The brothers initially focused on making a higher-quality product while offering restaurants a less expensive alternative to some premium options. They made the muffins themselves in Kyle's apartment and delivered them by hand. The brothers pooled $1,000 to buy a mixer and flour, with Meekins describing that as the entire initial investment.The company's early history is not described identically across sources. Stone & Skillet's current website says the founders created their recipe in their Boston apartment in 2013. Earlier reporting from WBUR in 2015 and 2017 identified Kyle Meekins and chef Dan Crothers as the company's co-founders, with Kyle saying he and Crothers developed the recipe together after restaurant chefs repeatedly asked for a better English muffin. More recent accounts, including Meekins' 2025 interview and the company's 2026 financing announcement, identify Cam, Kyle and Nick Meekins as the founders.The first major retail breakthrough came while the company was selling at a farmers market. Meekins told Entrepreneur that someone from Whole Foods discovered the product, leading the brothers to realise they could compete in retail as well as restaurants. WBUR's 2017 account similarly records Kyle saying a Whole Foods local forager approached them at the Boston Food Festival, after which the company began entering Whole Foods stores across the region.Meekins took over as CEO during the Covid pandemicMeekins became CEO of Stone & Skillet in 2020, during the Covid pandemic, after deciding to apply what he had learned from the music business to growing the food company. He had already spent years as a recording artist, having been signed with Atlantic Records and working in production, songwriting and performance. He said his experience in music gave him lessons that could be applied to building and promoting a consumer brand.The transition also followed a difficult period for the Meekins family. Their father, Russ Meekins, was described by Cam as a trusted adviser and best friend to the business before his death in 2020. Meekins said losing his father motivated him to focus all of his time on Stone & Skillet rather than continuing to divide his attention between music and the company.The company went from its first $100,000 month to 3,000 retail locationsStone & Skillet took months to establish consistent revenue. Meekins told Entrepreneur that in the early days, the brothers were happy when they sold through a batch of 20 packages. The company eventually reached its first $100,000 month during its second year, a milestone Meekins said made them realise they had built a real business. He also said the company had sold tens of millions of dollars in products over its history and described it as an eight-figure business.By 2026, the company had expanded to more than 3,000 retail locations across the US. Nutter, which represented Stone & Skillet in its Series A financing, lists Whole Foods Market, Publix, Wegmans and Fresh Thyme among its retail customers. The firm also confirmed that the company is headquartered in Boston and has achieved national distribution. In May 2026, Stone & Skillet announced a $5 million Series A led by BFG Partners, with Beliade Consumer Partners and Supernatural Ventures also participating. The company said the funding would support continued growth and expansion on the US West Coast.Meekins credits action and relationships for the journeyMeekins' advice to entrepreneurs centres on taking action, meeting people and remaining open to unexpected opportunities. He told Entrepreneur that founders should get out and build relationships because new connections can create opportunities that would otherwise be missed. He also stressed the value of surrounding yourself with people who know more about areas where you lack experience. His own career illustrates that approach. Rather than abandoning the skills he developed as a musician, Meekins applied lessons from promotion, relationships and audience-building to a consumer food company. Stone & Skillet's latest financing now gives the business additional capital for its next stage of expansion, including its push into the US West Coast. The company that began with a $1,000 investment and handmade muffins in a Boston apartment has since moved from hand-delivering products to restaurants to distributing through more than 3,000 retail locations across the country.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘PNS Hunain violated maritime norms’: India rejects Pakistan’s ‘usual prevarication’ over naval collision
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India on Friday rejected Pakistan’s allegations over the collision between Indian Navy warship INS Kolkata and Pakistan Navy vessel PNS Hun.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Friday rejected Pakistan’s allegations over the collision between Indian Navy warship INS Kolkata and Pakistan Navy vessel PNS Hunain in the Arabian Sea, accusing Islamabad of trying to “hide the truth” and saying the Pakistani vessel violated a 1991 bilateral agreement and international maritime regulations.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Pakistan's response to India's diplomatic protest was expected and rejected the allegations against India."Recent events involving Pakistan and India have taken place. I would like to clarify a few things before you. We have seen Pakistan's response to the protest lodged by us. As always, it is an evasive reply or an attempt to hide the truth, which was expected from them. We completely reject the allegations made against us. I would like to place some facts before you and reiterate them. INS Kolkata was on a routine deployment in the Western Arabian Sea when a Pakistani naval ship, PNS Hunain, behaved in an unacceptable and unprofessional manner at sea, resulting in a collision. The dangerous overtaking maneuver by PNS Hunain was a grave violation of Article 10 of the Agreement on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Maneuvers, and Troop Movements between India and Pakistan of April 1991. This article explicitly states that naval units in the sea should not come within three nautical miles of each other..."Jaiswal said the Pakistani vessel's manoeuvre also violated international maritime rules governing the prevention of collisions at sea."We have seen Pakistan's response to the protest we had lodged. It is the usual prevarication that we expected. We reject the allegations and insinuations contained therein. Let me reiterate the facts of the matter for you. INS Kolkata was on a routine deployment in the Western Arabian Sea when Pakistani naval ship Hunain conducted itself in an unacceptable and unprofessional manner at sea that resulted in a collision. The dangerous overtaking maneuver by PNS Hunain was in gross violation of Article 10 of the Agreement Between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Maneuvers and Troop Movements of 1991, which clearly specifies that naval units at sea are not to be within three nautical miles of each other. In addition, the Pakistani ship also infringed the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea. The Pakistani side has once again been advised about the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents. The incident did not cause any major damage to INS Kolkata, and she remains at sea..."What happened in the Arabian SeaThe collision took place on September 15 in the North Arabian Sea. India has said INS Kolkata was on routine deployment in international waters when PNS Hunain carried out a dangerous overtaking manoeuvre that resulted in the collision.Pakistan, however, has disputed India's account and accused the Indian warship of carrying out aggressive manoeuvres near its naval vessel. Islamabad has also claimed that the incident occurred within Pakistan's exclusive economic zone during its SEASPARK-26 naval exercise.Both countries have lodged diplomatic protests following the incident.Under Article 10 of the 1991 agreement between India and Pakistan, naval units at sea are required to maintain a separation of at least three nautical miles.India has maintained that PNS Hunain came close to INS Kolkata at high speed before the collision, describing the manoeuvre as a violation of the bilateral agreement as well as the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.India also said the incident did not cause major damage to INS Kolkata and that the warship remains at sea. Reports said PNS Hunain suffered damage and subsequently returned to port.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sway: Award-winning British rapper dies aged 44
articles.summary: Sway, whose hits included Still Speedin' and Level Up, was living in Ghana at the time of his death.
articles.body:
The award-winning British-Ghanaian rap artist Sway DaSafo has died at the age of 44.

He was the first unsigned rapper to win a Mobo Award in 2006, and scored a top 10 hit in 2012 with the single Level Up.

The news was first shared online by the Mobo organisation, and confirmed to the BBC by the musician's friend Kash Ahmad, who said he died at his home in Ghana.

Sway was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma in 2010 and went into remission later that year.

Sway was born Derek Andrew Safo in London, albeit accidentally, while his mother was on a stop-over between Amsterdam and her native Ghana.

After a brief period in her homeland, he was raised in north London and honed his craft on pirate radio. He credited the BBC's radio station 1Xtra with providing him with his first break in 2002.

Emerging during the first wave of grime, alongside artists such as Dizzee Rascal and Lethal Bizzle, he stood apart for his witty, literate style.

"I'm a positive person. The positivity comes out in my music," he told the Guardian as his career took off.

"I don't go round holding guns to people's heads so I won't rap about holding guns to people's heads."

Despite widespread interest from the music industry, he remained independent - releasing music on his own label, and selling mixtapes at markets and independent record shops.

He made headlines in September 2005 when he was named best hip-hop act at the Mobo awards - defeating US heavyweights such as 50 Cent and the Game.

The following year, he released his debut album This Is My Demo, accompanied by the top 40 single, Little Derek, which celebrated how he had "ended up in HMV instead of HMP".

Although the album stalled at number 78 in the charts, it earned him a nomination for the Mercury Prize, alongside acts like Arctic Monkeys and Muse.

In 2006, he supported The Streets on a UK tour and appeared alongside frontman Mike Skinner on the Mitchell Brothers' single Harvey Nicks.

But in 2010, DaSafo was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma.

"It felt like I had been dropped in the middle of the sea with no lifejacket," he later recalled.

"I didn't have time to think about how I was going to get to the other side, I just had to deal with it."

After receiving chemotherapy and radiotherapy, he went into remission, releasing his biggest hits Still Speedin' (which sampled Black Box's Ride On Time) and Level Up (featuring a verse from Kano) in 2012.

He enjoyed further critical and commercial success with albums including Deliverance, and Verses from the Vault; and collaborated with artists like Mark Ronson, Ed Sheeran, Akon and Childish Gambino.

Through his record label Dcypha, he also signed and developed artists including Tiggs Da Author and KSI.

All three appeared on the 2013 single No Sleep, and KSI went on to become a hugely successful YouTuber, with a sideline in music.

DaSafo also dabbled with an acting career, appearing in two episodes of the crime drama Top Boy and the 2012 film The Grind.

At the time of his death, he was working on new music. His final Instagram post, shared last week , celebrated his 44th birthday.

He is survived by two sons, Jalil and Ammar-Joseph, and twin daughters, Queen-Inaya and Queen-Imara. At the time of his death, he was raising them as a single parent in Ghana, his friend Kash Ahmad told BBC News.

"It was an honour and a pleasure to have known and worked with him, and my thoughts and prayers are with his family," he added.

Other tributes came from the Mitchell Brothers, who wrote: "We were privileged to have worked with you", and praised Sway's "true penmanship level and delivery".

"This hit me like a ton of bricks," said rapper and record label executive Kardinal Offishall. "Rest in eternal peace and God cover your babies. Til we meet again my friend."

So Solid Crew's Megaman simply posted "RIP"; while The Mobo Awards said they were "proud to have him as part of our history," adding: "Our love goes out to his family, loved ones and fans."

Rapper Baby Blue posted on Instagram: "In my heart I worried this day was coming but I wasn't prepared for the reality of losing Sway.

"He was my confidante and he guided me through so much of my life musically and personally... I will miss you forever my friend. I am lost."

Breaking the news to her listeners on BBC Radio 1Xtra, broadcaster Remi Burgz said it was a "sad day for British music" and called Sway a "UK Rap pioneer".

"One of north London's finest," she said, "he was mine and many others first experience of UK rap [and] hip-hop in mainstream media".

"He was a literal example of paving the way and showing that UK rap can take up space in music.

articles.title: Kildare: Gardaí 'acted appropriately' when pursuing car in M9 crash
articles.summary: Five teenage boys died in the head-on collision and four family members were seriously injured.
articles.body:
Irish police "acted appropriately" during its pursuit of a car which crashed on the wrong side of the road in the Republic of Ireland last month, the police watchdog has found.

Five teenage boys died in the head-on collision on the M9 and four family members were seriously injured in the crash on 16 August.

The police ombudsman Fiosrú said Gardaí (Irish police) had been following the car on the N78 in Athy for a short period before it joined the M9 motorway against the direction of traffic.

Police Ombudsman Emily Logan said the force acted "in line with relevant policies and procedures as determined by the Garda Commissioner".

The watchdog began its investigation into the incident after a mandatory referral from gardaí on 16 August 2026.

Their actions and decisions during interaction with the car were examined, including the nature and extent of garda contact prior to the collision.

The purpose of the investigation was to establish whether gardaí acted in accordance with the law and police policies and procedures.

The investigation found that on 16 August gardaí had pursued a BMW car after permission was granted by the Garda Control Room.

When the BMW entered the M9 dual carriageway the pursuit was terminated and the control room confirmed that it shouldn't continue.

Other garda units attempted to place a stopping device at an appropriate location, however the BMW undertook a number of U-turns, before fatally colliding with an oncoming car.

The five boys in the BMW died and the four family members in the car it collided with were seriously injured.

Logan added that when "someone dies in incidents involving contact with gardaí, it is mandatory that the matter is referred by gardaí to Fiosrú to investigate".

"Fiosrú's investigation was independent of gardaí and aimed to understand events leading up to the collision.

"My thoughts are with family and friends and all those affected by this devastating incident, including the gardaí who attended the scene."

The M9 incident is the sixth time a garda interaction with vehicles driving on the wrong side of the road has been reported between 2021 and 2026.

articles.title: Hot meals for Jersey primary schools to be supplied by UK company
articles.summary: The government says Apetito Limited were selected after an "open and compliant procurement process".
articles.body:
A food company from the UK has been appointed to provide hot school meals for government primary schools across Jersey.

Education minister deputy Catherine Curtis said she had signed a contract with Apetito Limited to also provide menu development, meal production, nutritional compliance and associated catering services.

The School Food Programme began as a pilot in 2019 in partnership with local charity Caring Cooks and Apetito Limited joined it in 2024.

The government said the Wiltshire food firm had been selected following an "open and compliant" procurement process which had included evaluating quality, service delivery arrangements, sustainability and price.

Apetito Limited had demonstrated "a clear ability to meet the nutritional, operational, and logistical requirements of the School Food Programme, as well as the capacity to deliver meals at scale," it said.

The government added fresh fruit supplied by Valley Foods in St Martin would replace a dessert option twice a week.

articles.title: 'Hate needs to stop': Indian-origin US lawmaker 'horrified' after Sikh driver stabbed 17 times in Wyoming
articles.summary: US News: Indian-origin US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi has condemned the stabbing of a Sikh truck driver in Wyoming, saying the attack comes amid what he de.
articles.body: Indian-origin US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi has condemned the stabbing of a Sikh truck driver in Wyoming, saying the attack comes amid what he described as rising hatred targeting Sikh and South Asian Americans in the US.His remarks also referred to a recent Trump administration post featuring a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and telling him to “get off our roads” and “self-deport”.Krishnamoorthi said he was “horrified” by the attack on the truck driver, who was stabbed 17 times at a rest stop in Wyoming. He added that Americans should stand against both hate and violence.“Those spreading this hate, including officials in our own federal government, need to stop. Those who turn it into violence must be held accountable,” the Democratic congressman said in a post on X.Krishnamoorthi, meanwhile, called for those responsible for the attack to be held accountable and said Americans should stand against both hate and violence.Sikh truck driver stabbed 17 timesThe victim, identified as 28-year-old Gurvinder Singh, an Indian-origin Punjabi Sikh truck driver from Sacramento, was attacked on September 13 at the Bitter Creek Rest Area along Interstate 80 in Wyoming.Singh told NPR that he had stopped at the rest area while travelling towards Pennsylvania when another man followed him into a washroom and suddenly attacked him with a knife. He suffered multiple stab wounds to his neck, chest, arms and ribs before managing to escape the restroom and call for help.A family at the rest area heard Singh crying for help and came to his assistance. The family also provided police with information about the suspect's vehicle.The Wyoming Highway Patrol later stopped the vehicle near Rawlins and arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak, 45. He has been charged with attempted first-degree murder. Authorities have not established a motive for the attack.Singh, who has been driving trucks commercially for around three years, said the incident has left him concerned about the safety of other Punjabi Sikh truck drivers travelling across the US.What was the ‘Mr Singh’ post?Krishnamoorthi's comments came days after the US Department of Homeland Security faced criticism over an AI-generated graphic featuring a brown-skinned, bearded Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh”.The graphic, posted as part of the Trump administration's messaging on illegal immigration and immigrant truck drivers, carried the message: “America for Americans. Get off our roads; you don't know how to drive, Mr Singh.” It also urged immigrants to “self-deport”.The DHS post was later removed following criticism from Sikh and Indian-American organisations.The American Sikh Council has called for a full and transparent investigation into the Wyoming stabbing, requesting authorities to examine whether race, religion or identity played any role in the attack.The group has also stressed that it is not claiming that the DHS post caused or triggered the stabbing, as there is currently no evidence establishing such a connection.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ex-Labour deputy leader Tom Watson joins Palantir
articles.summary: Lord Watson praises his new employers but says there are "legitimate questions" about big tech firms that "require answers".
articles.body:
Former cabinet minister and Labour Party deputy leader Lord Tom Watson has become a senior vice president at US tech firm Palantir.

Announcing his appointment on X, Lord Watson said Palantir was "the most interesting company on the planet, doing work of real consequence".

He said the company had "challenges" and that while some criticism was "propaganda" there were "legitimate questions about large technology companies and sovereign control".

Green MP Sian Berry said: "This is yet another example of the corrosive revolving door between politics and big business lobbying that has no place in public life."

She added: "Palantir, with its work for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) in the US and the IDF (Israel Defense Forces), has no business at all in our NHS and public services.

"Tom Watson has been employed to lobby his friends in the Labour government."

Palantir builds software aimed at allowing organisations to make better use of their data and holds a large number of UK government contracts including with the NHS, the Ministry of Defence and 11 police forces.

The company has attracted controversy, with some MPs calling for more scrutiny of its use of data within NHS contracts.

Palantir is currently involved in a legal battle with the Mayor of London's office, over its decision to block the Metropolitan Police from agreeing a contract with the company.

The Mayor's Office said it was not satisfied the deal adequately ensured value for money but also raised concern about the firm's values.

Palantir has argued that its software has improved NHS databases in a number of areas such as waiting lists and hospital supplies, while its work with police forces has helped tackle corruption and identify women at risk of domestic violence.

Louis Mosley, head of UK and Europe at Palantir Technologies, welcomed the appointment of Lord Watson saying he brought a "deep understanding of how AI is changing the ways the state can help people in Britain, where more than one in six Palantirians are based".

Lord Watson was a Labour MP for more than 20 years and became a senior figure in the party, serving as a minister as well as a key behind-the-scenes operator, who reportedly orchestrated efforts to remove Tony Blair as prime minister.

In 2015, he was strongly criticised for publicising unsubstantiated claims of sex abuse by the Conservative politician Leon Brittan.

Brittan died before learning that the police had dropped their investigation and that he had no case to answer.

At the time, Lord Watson said he was "sorry for the distress Leon Brittan's family experienced" but that he felt he had a "duty" to report claims.

After leaving the House of Commons he was given a peerage and took up a position as the chair of UK Music.

In a statement, he said Palantir was "helping Britain and its allies defend themselves, helping police protect our citizens and helping NHS staff get patients treated and home sooner".

"We have challenges. Some criticism is propaganda. Some raises legitimate questions about large technology companies and sovereign control. Both require answers.

"Part of my role will be to correct false information while working with our engineers to ensure privacy, security and respect for sovereignty are at the heart of everything we do."
