articles.title: Meet Joe Petraro-Hyppolite: 13-year-old New York boy who scored 1,590 on SAT and is set to pursue a master's at NYU, with a reported IQ of 168
articles.summary: US News: Joe Petraro-Hyppolite, a 13-year-old from Long Island, New York, is preparing to begin a master's programme at New York University in 2027. His academ.
articles.body: Joe Petraro-Hyppolite, a 13-year-old from Long Island, New York, is preparing to begin a master's programme at New York University in 2027. His academic journey has attracted attention after he reportedly scored 1,590 out of 1,600 on the SAT at the age of 10 and earned his high school diploma at 11. He is currently working towards an undergraduate degree and plans to graduate in May 2027. Joe has an IQ of 168 and has also attended Louisiana State University. His planned master's programme will focus on sports management, while kinesiology and biology are among his other academic interests. Alongside his education, he volunteers at a nursing home and hopes to become a palaeontologist.Joe Petraro-Hyppolite’s remarkable academic journeyPetraro-Hyppolite achieved several academic milestones at an unusually young age. He scored 1,590 on the SAT at 10 and received his high school diploma at 11. He later attended Louisiana State University and continued working towards his undergraduate degree alongside considerably older students. His academic progress has allowed him to pursue university education during his early teens. The SAT has a maximum score of 1,600, placing his reported result 10 points below the highest possible score.Petraro-Hyppolite told CBS News New York that he had been accepted into a master's programme at New York University and planned to begin in 2027. He said his master's would be in sports management and also mentioned kinesiology and biology. He is expected to complete his undergraduate degree in May 2027 before starting postgraduate studies at NYU.Teenager discusses learning and reported IQ of 168Petraro-Hyppolite has spoken about his learning process and the effort involved in managing an accelerated academic journey. Despite his reported IQ of 168, he said that he still needs to study and understand material before retaining it. “It’s not like I was shot out the womb knowing everything I know. I have to learn it once or twice. Then I’ll know,” he said. Joe also described feeling nervous and excited about the next stage of his education, as he prepares to take on new academic challenges.His mother recalls his earlier educational experienceHis mother, Anne Petraro-Hyppolite, said her son's progress was particularly meaningful because he had previously been placed in special education classes after being diagnosed with Tourette syndrome. The condition is a neurological disorder associated with motor and vocal tics. Speaking about her son's achievements, she said, “It's just surreal. When he graduated high school so young, it was surreal, but this is ... everything he does is surreal. He just loves to learn. He is like a sponge.”Volunteering and ambitions beyond universityAlongside his studies, Petraro-Hyppolite volunteers at a nursing home in the Five Towns area of Long Island, where he helps residents. Although he plans to pursue a master's in sports management, Joe has also expressed an ambition to become a palaeontologist in the future. His interests extend across sports, biology and prehistoric life. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror had no doubt she deliberately killed her children
articles.summary: It is the first time the juror, who refused to side with the others and acquit Clancy, has spoken publicly about his decision.
articles.body:
The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.

Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.

To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.

The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.

Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.

Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.

"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.

"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."

'Emotional rollercoaster' - Lindsay Clancy jurors speak out on what led to mistrial

What happens next after Lindsay Clancy's murder case ends in a mistrial?

Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.

"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.

The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".

She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."

Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".

But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.

The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.

Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.

In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.

He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".

During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.

Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.

A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.

However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions , while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.

The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.

Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.

He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.

He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."

The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

articles.title: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
articles.summary: Police reportedly fired into the air on Friday morning as they struggled to contain crowds jostling to secure a place at the tented site.
articles.body:
Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.

Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.

Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.

Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave.

The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.

During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.

More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.

The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.

The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis.

Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker".

"The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said.

The opposition also accused Sánchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. Sánchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents , its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened.

Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died".

The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for Sánchez.

The prime minister is at odds with Italy , with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco.

The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.

After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds.

Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities.

articles.title: 1,000-year-old church mystery cracked by students from King Charles' alma mater
articles.summary: Gordonstoun students in Scotland uncovered altar foundations inside ruins on the deserted island of Swona in Orkney, revealing a likely Viking-era church.
articles.body: Boarding school students in Scotland helped uncover something extraordinary during a school trip: the remains of what's believed to be a 1,000-year-old Viking-era church. Young people from Gordonstoun, located in Moray, Scotland, uncovered the foundations of an altar and a step inside the long-known ruins on the deserted island of Swona in Orkney. Gordonstoun — the alma mater of King Charles III and his late father, Prince Philip — runs an annual service project on the remote island called the Swona Service Project, where students take part in archaeological and restoration work. ANCIENT VIKING SWORD DISCOVERED 'STICKING UP OUT OF THE GROUND' AFTER 1,300 YEARS Gordonstoun housemaster Daniel McLean, who is also the organizer of the project, told Fox News Digital the structure had long been known locally as a "kirk," or church, but its origins remained uncertain. While the ruins themselves were already known, it was unclear whether the structure had actually been a church. The excavation uncovered altar foundations and a step, lending new weight to a local legend that the ruins were once a church. The team had surveyed the site the previous year, McLean said, and found several characteristics consistent with early medieval church architecture. 'SIGNIFICANT' EARLY CHRISTIAN CHURCH EMERGES BENEATH FORMER FISH MARKET IN ANCIENT CITY "Everything about the structure [fit]," he said. "The size of it, the length, the width ratio, the east-west orientation, the location of the door, the construction methods — it all [fit] for it to be an early medieval church." When the team returned to excavate the site, McLean said they began digging along the inside of the eastern wall, where they believed an altar would have stood. "I thought if there's anything churchy here, we may find the remains of where the altar was on the inside of the east wall," McLean said. The team quickly uncovered the foundations of the altar and a step in front of it. RARE ROYAL ARTIFACT LINKED TO INFLUENTIAL KING-TURNED-SAINT UNCOVERED AFTER DECADES MISSING The church is believed to date to the 10th or 11th century, based on similarities to other Viking-era churches in the region. For Archie Maclean, one of the students who worked on the excavation, seeing the remains up close made the discovery feel real. "The structure of the building is still so visible, even after years of earth and wind and weather eroding the outside." "When you see the altar in person, you go, 'Oh my gosh, it's still an altar after all of this time,'" Maclean told Fox News Digital. Maclean helped dig the original test pit and later cleaned up the altar and doorway for photographs. He said he was struck by how well the structure had survived. DISCOVERY BENEATH SOCCER FIELD REVEALS MASSIVE MEDIEVAL CONVENT LOST FOR CENTURIES "Same with the doorway as well, the structure of the building is still so visible, even after years of earth and wind and weather eroding the outside — I found [it] fascinating personally," Maclean said. The school has a unique arrangement with the island's owners, the Annal family, and the Swona Heritage Group, to make the experience possible. The 10 students traveled roughly 10 hours by bus, ferry and boat to reach Swona, a remote island about seven miles north of John o' Groats. Alfie Pullin, a student who helped restore the old house where the group stayed, told Fox News Digital the team worked to replace its wooden living room floor, which had rotted away because of drainage problems. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The house had no electricity, while the students pumped fresh water from a 1,000-year-old well, according to Gordonstoun. Pullin described spending a week working on the isolated island without knowing what the experience would bring as "very surreal." "I think it's very surreal to go onto an island with a task, but also a sense of [not knowing] what will actually happen while you're on there for a week," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Pullin added the experience allowed the students "to make these discoveries and to upkeep the island and come away knowing more and leaving the island in a better state than it was before." School officials plan to return to Swona next year for further investigations of the archaeological sites. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The team also plans to use GPS data and digital images collected at the site to create a 3D model of the church, while archaeologists hope further analysis will help determine its age. Maclean said discoveries on remote sites such as Swona can provide clues about the communities that once lived there, as well as how Christianity spread. articles.title: Michael Sheen had 'constructive' meeting with first minister over toxic dumping claims
articles.summary: Michael Sheen said his meeting with the first minister was "early days but that's really encouraging".
articles.body:
Hollywood actor Michael Sheen said he had a "constructive" meeting with First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth over toxic dumping claims raised in his BBC documentary.

Sheen initially said an offer to meet the first minister "was not taken up" before the documentary was broadcast in August.

On Thursday, the Welsh actor said he met the first minister, speaking about how they could move forward adding it was "early days but that's really encouraging".

Speaking on Instagram , he said "I've just come from a meeting with the first minister.

"Talking about how we can move forward and address all the issues that Buried [the documentary] raised around the toxic dumping, and that was really constructive.

"So early days but that's really encouraging."

In the UK Parliament last week, Sheen urged MPs to back a national testing programme for historic toxic dumps to make sure sites were safe, after high levels of cancer-causing chemicals - known as PCBs - were found in soil samples and in the blood of people living near sites linked to chemical giant Monsanto.

Sheen interviewed farming consultant turned campaigner Douglas Gowan shortly before his death, who had spent decades warning that communities were at risk of toxic chemicals.

The actor later teamed up with investigative journalists Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby who had inherited all of the campaigner's documents and research.

They set about testing 14 sites in Wales and north west England where it was thought Monsanto had been dumping PCBs, and found elevated levels at all but one.

Susan Smith, who worked at Monsanto in Wrexham, said her happy memories of working there have been replaced with fears following the documentary.

Susan and her husband Geraint's home, which they have lived in for 53 years, is separated from the decommissioned Ruabon chemical works by a thin tree line.

Geraint was diagnosed with prostate cancer 13 years ago before more recently developing skin cancer, while Susan developed breast cancer when she was 38.

While they admit they are not certain that Monsanto was responsible, the documentary has made them question the possible impact of the factory on their family's health.

Susan worked as a secretary for four years when she was 19, then returned once for temporary cover and another time to overhaul a failing system.

"Most of my time was spent in the telex office next to the warehouse. We used to send delivery notes, instructions, requests on little pieces of ticker tape through a machine to other Monsanto offices," she said.

"We had a small glass hatch that the instructions would be passed through and it was never closed because people were passing things through so often. As a result dust and powders and all sorts would blow through and coat the desks, the paper, even our sandwiches."

Susan said she wasn't given a "safety briefing, protective clothing or anything" and office staff never knew they were at risk.

Susan had her blood tested by the documentary team and while the PCB levels in her blood were not deemed high, the fact there is no safe level of PCB and the lack of accountability from Eastman – the US company which now owns what was once Monsanto – has left her with unanswered questions.

The couple have joined the Monsanto Contamination Action Group – which was set up for people in Wrexham who live in communities affected by historic industrial waste dumping.
